name: Zeek Intrusion Detection — Beaconing, DNS Exfil, TLS Exfil & PsExec
description: Zeek-based intrusion detection using conn.log, dns.log, smb_files.log, and dce_rpc.log. Key techniques: beaconing detection via regular conn.log connection intervals (PowerShell Empire every 5s), DNS exfiltration via high-entropy subdomain enumeration in dns.log, TLS exfiltration via datamash byte-sum one-liner revealing ~270MB to suspicious host, PsExec detection via PSEXESVC.exe in smb_files.log + svcctl CreateServiceW in dce_rpc.log.
notes:
=== EXAMPLE 1: BEACONING DETECTION (PowerShell Empire) ===
Indicator: malware beaconing = periodic, regular outbound connections to C2

PCAP: /home/htb-student/pcaps/psempire.pcap
Tool: /usr/local/zeek/bin/zeek -C -r /home/htb-student/pcaps/psempire.pcap

What to look for in conn.log:
  → Multiple TCP connections to same destination IP:port
  → Regular intervals between connection timestamps
  → Similar orig_bytes and resp_bytes per connection (fixed payload size)
  → conn_state: SF (normal established + closed = successful C2 beacon)

Beaconing IOC:
  Source: 192.168.56.14
  Destination: 51.15.197.127:80
  Interval: ~5 seconds between ts fields
  orig_bytes: 199-208 (small, fixed-size requests)
  resp_bytes: 399 (consistent responses)
  → Empire default beacon interval: 5 seconds

Analysis command:
  cat conn.log   → read and look at ts column differences for regular intervals
  → If timestamps show 5.xxx seconds between each connection = beaconing

Zeek vs Suricata: Suricata caught the Empire rule; Zeek shows the timing pattern

=== EXAMPLE 2: DNS EXFILTRATION ===
Indicator: data exfil via DNS subdomains — encoded data in subdomain queries

PCAP: /home/htb-student/pcaps/dnsexfil.pcapng
Tool: /usr/local/zeek/bin/zeek -C -r /home/htb-student/pcaps/dnsexfil.pcapng

Analysis commands:
  cat dns.log | /usr/local/zeek/bin/zeek-cut query | cut -d . -f1-7
    → Extracts query field from all DNS entries
    → cut -d . -f1-7: show first 7 dot-separated parts of domain name

What to look for in dns.log:
  → One domain (letsgohunt.online) with hundreds of unique subdomains
  → Subdomain prefixes: www.1204192da26d109d4.*, cdn.0600553f0.*, post.1460.*
  → Pattern: hex strings encoded as subdomain labels
  → Not typical cloud CDN behavior — legitimate CDNs use consistent hostnames

DNS tunneling patterns:
  Exfil in query:  data.<chunk>.<domain> (high-entropy subdomain)
  Exfil in response: TXT record with encoded data
  DGA C2: random-looking subdomains of registered domain (sgtqrgcask.windomain.local)

Exfil IOCs in dns.log:
  → Single domain with 50+ unique subdomains in short timeframe
  → Subdomain labels contain hex/base64 strings (not real words)
  → Queries use prefixes like 'www.', 'cdn.', 'post.' followed by entropy
  → Many NOERROR responses to hex-string queries (server is controlled by attacker)

=== EXAMPLE 3: TLS EXFILTRATION ===
Indicator: large amount of data sent to external IP over TLS

PCAP: /home/htb-student/pcaps/tlsexfil.pcap
Tool: /usr/local/zeek/bin/zeek -C -r /home/htb-student/pcaps/tlsexfil.pcap

Byte-sum one-liner:
  cat conn.log | /usr/local/zeek/bin/zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h orig_bytes \
    | sort | grep -v -e '^$' | grep -v '-' \
    | datamash -g 1,2 sum 3 | sort -k 3 -rn | head -10

Command breakdown:
  zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h orig_bytes → extract src IP, dst IP, bytes from src
  sort                                     → sort lines for grouping
  grep -v -e '^$'                          → remove empty lines
  grep -v '-'                              → remove lines with '-' (missing Zeek field)
  datamash -g 1,2 sum 3                   → group by col1+col2, sum col3
  sort -k 3 -rn                           → sort by bytes (col3) descending
  head -10                                 → top 10 src→dst pairs by volume

Result:
  10.0.10.100    192.168.151.181    270775912
  → ~270 MB sent from internal host to 192.168.151.181
  → 270 MB over SSL to same IP = strong exfiltration IOC

TLS exfil IOCs in conn.log:
  → One external IP receiving massive orig_bytes (100MB+)
  → Many persistent TLS connections to same destination
  → Service field: ssl (port 443)
  → Compare against baseline — legitimate cloud services also have high bytes

=== EXAMPLE 4: PSEXEC DETECTION ===
Indicator: PsExec uploads PSEXESVC.exe to ADMIN$ share, then creates temp service via IPC$

PCAP: /home/htb-student/pcaps/psexec_add_user.pcap
Tool: /usr/local/zeek/bin/zeek -C -r /home/htb-student/pcaps/psexec_add_user.pcap

Logs to check: smb_files.log + dce_rpc.log + smb_mapping.log

smb_files.log — what to look for:
  → action: SMB::FILE_OPEN on \\dc1\ADMIN$ for PSEXESVC.exe   ← upload indicator
  → action: SMB::FILE_DELETE on \\dc1\ADMIN$ for PSEXESVC.exe ← cleanup after
  → size: 145568 (PSEXESVC.exe binary)

dce_rpc.log — what to look for:
  → endpoint: svcctl (Service Control Manager over named pipe)
  → named_pipe: \\pipe\\ntsvcs
  → operations in sequence:
    1. OpenSCManagerW   ← connect to SCM
    2. CreateServiceWOW64W ← create temp service = PSEXESVC
    3. OpenServiceW
    4. StartServiceW    ← start the service (executes command)
    5. QueryServiceStatus
    6. ControlService   ← stop the service
    7. DeleteService    ← remove temp service
    8. CloseServiceHandle

smb_mapping.log — what to look for:
  → \\dc1\ADMIN$  DISK  ← file upload to ADMIN share
  → \\dc1\IPC$    PIPE  ← service creation via IPC pipe

PsExec attack flow:
  1. Attacker authenticates to SMB (445)
  2. Connects to \\target\ADMIN$ — uploads PSEXESVC.exe
  3. Connects to \\target\IPC$ — uses svcctl to create + start PSEXESVC service
  4. Service executes attacker's command (net user hacker /add, etc.)
  5. Service stopped and deleted; PSEXESVC.exe deleted

MITRE: T1543.003 (Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service)
MITRE: T1570 (Lateral Tool Transfer)
PCAP source: https://github.com/401TRG/detections/raw/master/pcaps/20171220_smb_psexec_add_user.pcap
